In [[mathematical analysis]], '''Wiener's Tauberian theorem''' is any of several related results [[Mathematical proof|proved]] by [[Norbert Wiener]] in 1932.<ref>See {{harvtxt|Wiener|1932}}.</ref> They provide a necessary and sufficient condition under which any [[Function (mathematics)|function]] in [[Lp space|<math>L^1</math> or <math>L^2</math>]] 
can be approximated by [[linear combination]]s of [[Shift operator|translations]] of a given function.<ref>see {{harvtxt|Rudin|1991}}.</ref>

Informally, if the [[Fourier transform]] of a function <math>f</math> vanishes on a certain set <math>Z</math>, the Fourier transform of any linear combination of translations of <math>f</math> also vanishes on <math>Z</math>. Therefore, the linear combinations of translations of <math>f</math> cannot approximate a function whose Fourier transform does not vanish 
on <math>Z</math>.

Wiener's theorems make this precise, stating that linear combinations of translations of <math>f</math> are [[dense set|dense]] [[if and only if]] the [[zero set]] of the Fourier 
transform of <math>f</math> is [[empty set|empty]] (in the case of <math>L^1</math>) or of [[Lebesgue measure]] zero (in the case of <math>L^2</math>).

[[Israel Gelfand|Gelfand]] reformulated Wiener's theorem in terms of [[commutative C*-algebra]]s, when it states that the spectrum of the <math>L^1</math> group ring 
<math>L^1(\mathbb{R})</math> of the [[mathematics|group]] <math>\mathbb{R}</math> of [[real number]]s is the dual group of <math>\mathbb{R}</math>. A similar result is true when 
<math>\mathbb{R}</math> is replaced by any [[locally compact abelian group]].

== Introduction ==
A typical Tauberian theorem is the following result, for <math>f\in L^1(0,\infty)</math>.  If:
# <math>f(x)=O(1)</math> as <math>x\to\infty</math>
# <math>\frac1x\int_0^\infty e^{-t/x}f(t)\,dt \to L</math> as <math>x\to\infty</math>, 
then
:<math>\frac1x\int_0^xf(t)\,dt \to L.</math>

Generalizing, let <math>G(t)</math> be a given function, and <math>P_G(f)</math> be the proposition
:<math>\frac1x\int_0^\infty G(t/x)f(t)\,dt \to L.</math>
Note that one of the hypotheses and the conclusion of the Tauberian theorem has the form <math>P_G(f)</math>, respectively, with <math>G(t)=e^{-t}</math> and <math>G(t)=1_{[0,1]}(t).</math>
The second hypothesis is a "Tauberian condition".

Wiener's Tauberian theorems have the following structure:<ref>{{citation|author=[[G H Hardy]]|title=Divergent series}}, pp 385-377</ref>
:If <math>G_1</math> is a given function such that <math>W(G_1)</math>, <math>P_{G_1}(f)</math>, and <math>R(f)</math>, then <math>P_{G_2}(f)</math> holds for all "reasonable" <math>G_2</math>.
Here <math>R(f)</math> is a "Tauberian" condition on <math>f</math>, and <math>W(G_1)</math> is a special condition on the kernel <math>G_1</math>.  The power of the theorem is that <math>P_{G_2}(f)</math> holds, not for a particular kernel <math>G_2</math>, but for ''all'' reasonable kernels <math>G_2</math>.

The Wiener condition is roughly a condition on the zeros the Fourier transform of <math>G_2</math>.  For instance, for functions of class <math>L^1</math>, the condition is that the Fourier transform does not vanish anywhere.  This condition is often easily seen to be a ''necessary'' condition for a Tauberian theorem of this kind to hold.  The key point is that this easy [[Necessity and sufficiency|necessary condition]] is also sufficient.

==The condition in {{math|''L''<sup>1</sup>}}==

Let <math>f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})</math> be an [[integrable function]]. The [[linear span|span]] of translations <math>f_a(x) = f(x+a)</math>
is dense in <math>L^1(\mathbb{R})</math> if and only if the Fourier transform of <math>f</math> has no real [[zero of a function|zeros]].

===Tauberian reformulation===

The following statement is equivalent to the previous result,{{Citation needed|date=October 2018}} and explains why Wiener's result is a [[Tauberian theorem]]:

Suppose the Fourier transform of <math>f\in L^1</math> has no real zeros, and suppose the [[convolution]] 
<math>f*h</math> tends to zero at infinity for some <math>h\in L^\infty</math>. Then the convolution <math>g*h</math> tends to zero at infinity for any
<math>g\in L^1</math>.

More generally, if

: <math>\lim_{x \to \infty} (f*h)(x) = A \int f(x) \,dx</math>

for some <math>f\in L^1</math> the Fourier transform of which has no real zeros, then also

: <math>\lim_{x \to \infty} (g*h)(x) = A \int g(x) \,dx</math>

for any <math>g\in  L^1</math>.

===Discrete version===

Wiener's theorem has a counterpart in 
<math>l^1(\mathbb{Z})</math>: the span of the translations of <math>f\in  l^1(\mathbb{Z})</math> is dense if and only if the Fourier transform

:<math>\varphi(\theta) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} f(n) e^{-in\theta} \,</math>

has no real zeros. The following statements are equivalent version of this result:

* Suppose the Fourier transform of <math>f\in l^1(\mathbb{Z})</math> has no real zeros, and for some bounded sequence <math>h</math> the convolution <math>f*h</math>
tends to zero at infinity. Then <math>g*h</math> also tends to zero at infinity for any <math>g\in  l^1(\mathbb{Z})</math>.
* Let <math>\varphi</math> be a function on the [[unit circle]] with [[Absolute convergence|absolutely convergent]] [[Fourier series]]. Then <math>1/\varphi</math> has absolutely convergent Fourier series 
if and only if <math>\varphi</math> has no zeros.

{{harvs|txt|last=Gelfand|year1=1941a|year2=1941b}} showed that this is equivalent to the following property of the [[Wiener algebra]] <math>A(\mathbb{T})</math>, 
which he proved using the theory of [[Banach algebra]]s, thereby giving a new proof of Wiener's result:

* The [[maximal ideal]]s of <math>A(\mathbb{T})</math> are all of the form

::<math>M_x = \left\{ f \in A(\mathbb{T}) \mid f(x) = 0 \right\}, \quad x \in \mathbb{T}.</math>

==The condition in {{math|''L''<sup>2</sup>}}==

Let <math>f\in L^2(\mathbb{R})</math> be a [[square-integrable function]]. The span of translations <math>f_a(x) = f(x+a) </math> is dense in <math>L^2(\mathbb{R})</math>
if and only if the real zeros of the Fourier transform of <math>f</math> form a set of [[Lebesgue measure#Null sets|zero Lebesgue measure]].

The parallel statement in <math>l^2(\mathbb{Z})</math> is as follows: the span of translations of a sequence <math>f\in l^2(\mathbb{Z})</math> is dense if and only if the zero set of the Fourier transform

:<math>\varphi(\theta) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} f(n) e^{-in\theta}</math>

has zero Lebesgue measure.
